newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland talks await Blair-Trimble showdown.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland talks await Blair-Trimble showdown.

text.p: Northern Ireland's fragile peace process awaited the outcome on Monday of a showdown over IRA arms between its most powerful pro-British politician, David Trimble, and British Prime Minister Tony Blair.

Trimble's Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) is furious that Sinn Fein will be admitted to Belfast peace talks after its IRA guerrilla allies called a halt to their 28-year war against British rule of the province at the weekend.
A Trimble ally, the UK Unionist party, announced that it was pulling out of the year-old talks in protest at what its leader, Robert McCartney, called "terror appeasement" by Britain.
He made the announcement at Belfast's Stormont buildings moments after a Sinn Fein delegation arrived to occupy offices in the ornate parkland complex to take part in the talks.

It was the first time Sinn Fein had been allowed to enter the buildings. The Irish republican party was banned from the talks until the IRA ceasefire and will be permitted to take part in negotiations in six weeks if Britain says the truce is real.

McCartney said his party, one of three unionist groups committed to British rule of the province, would take no further part in the negotiations except to vote against Britiain's plan to "decommission" arms at a talks' session on Wednesday.
A second unionist group, the Democratic Unionist Party of Ian Paisley, is also threatening to walk out of the talks, which are co-sponsored by Britain and Ireland.

Under British proposals, the Irish Republican Army and other guerrilla groups will not have to surrender weapons to gain representation at the talks but must discuss the issue in a sub-committee alongside political negotiations.

Trimble, in his first public comment on the IRA truce, was sharply critical of the government's Northern Ireland office for proposing that Sinn Fein be allowed to take part in negotiations before the IRA hands over a single weapon.
"We are dealing with duplicity from the Northern Ireland office on a massive scale," Trimble told BBC Radio Ulster.
But he stopped short of threatening to walk out of the Belfast talks if he did not get Blair to agree that the IRA should "decommission" its arsenal.
Mitchel McLaughlin, Sinn Fein's chairman, said of Trimble's position:"It is an incredible decision to adopt that the peace process is over because the IRA has called a cessation."

He played down concerns that all three unionist parties might boycott the talks, which would rob them of the consensus required by ground rules to negotiate any settlement between unionists and Irish nationalists.
"I believe those who walk out of the talks will return. The door should be left open so that that can happen," he told reporters when he arrived at Stormont to inspect the offices.
Trimble said the IRA had called the truce because Sinn Fein had been given to understand by Britain that it would not have to secure the handover of any IRA arms during the talks.
"They (Sinn Fein) interpret is as a guarantee that they don't have to carry out any decommissioning at all," he said.
McLaughlin said his understanding was that decommissioning would be part of a final settlement.
"Sinn Fein's view is that we will have decommissioning as part of a comprehensive negotiated agreement," McLaughlin said.

British officials allowed the Sinn Fein delegation, led by a man convicted of bombing for the IRA in the 1970s, to enter the premises where the year-long negotiations have faltered for 13 months over the decommissioning issue.

Gerry Kelly, who was jailed for bombing London's Old Bailey court complex in 1972, said he and his aides had come to occupy their offices after the IRA ceasefire and hoped to hold preliminary talks with other parties to the negotiations.
Kelly is a senior official in Sinn Fein. He escaped from a British jail in the 1980s,was extradited from the Netherlands and has been on the party's negotiating team ever since.
The moment was full of symbolism for Sinn Fein. Its leaders, Gerry Adams and Martin McGuinness, have twice been refused entry to Stormont in the past year when they tried to join the talks.
Britain refused them entry and has cut off contact with the party because of the IRA's refusal to to renew a truce the guerrillas called in August ,1994, and broke in February 1996.

But Sinn Fein's entry was overshadowed by Trimble's talks with Blair which could decide whether the negotiations focus again on decommissioning or start searching for a negotiated settlement to a conflict that has killed 3,200.
